messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Security Guard
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 49

**Patient Vignette: Mr. D.**

Mr. D. is a 71-year-old married man, a former construction foreman who now works as a night security guard at a suburban office park. He presents as a stout, quietly intense man, his hands calloused and his posture rigid. He has been married to his wife, Helen, for forty-eight years. He came to therapy at her insistence, though he is quick to say, “I don’t have a problem. I just have a life.”

The trauma happened twenty-three years ago, on a Tuesday morning in April. Mr. D. was sixty years old, working as a foreman on a high-rise project in a major city. He was on the ground floor, checking a delivery manifest, when the bomb went off. He doesn’t remember the sound. He remembers the *push*—a wall of air that threw him against a concrete pillar. He remembers the silence that followed, a high, ringing silence, and then the dust. It was not gray dust. It was a fine, white, choking powder that coated everything, that filled his mouth and nose, that made the world look like a snow globe after someone has shaken it.

He remembers pulling a man from the rubble, a young electrician named Rico. Rico’s leg was pinned. Mr. D. remembers the wet, heavy feel of the debris, the way Rico’s shouts turned into a low, animal moan. He remembers the second wave of sound—the sirens—and the sight of a woman’s shoe, still laced, lying perfectly alone on a pile of broken glass.

He did not talk about it. Not to anyone. He went back to work two weeks later. He finished the building. He retired at sixty-five, and took the security job because he couldn’t stand being home. “Helen wants to talk,” he says. “About nothing. About the garden. I can’t listen to it.”

In the present, Mr. D. works the graveyard shift, 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. He patrols a half-empty office complex. He says he likes the quiet. But in session, he describes a ritual he cannot break: every forty-five minutes, he must shine his flashlight into every single window of every single car in the parking lot. He knows it’s unnecessary. He knows the lot is empty. But the thought of skipping a single car makes his chest tighten. He feels a pressure behind his eyes, a sense that if he doesn’t look, something terrible will happen. “It’s just being thorough,” he says, but his jaw is clenched.

He sleeps in a recliner in the living room. He has not slept in the same bed as his wife in eight years. He says it’s because of his back. But the real reason is the dreams. He doesn’t call them nightmares. He calls them “the show.” In the show, he is always in the dust. He can’t breathe. He is searching for Rico, but Rico is not a man anymore—he is a pile of shoes. Mr. D. wakes up with his heart pounding, drenched in sweat, and he cannot go back to sleep. He says he is not afraid of the dream. He is afraid of *going back* to sleep.

He has become hypervigilant in a way that isolates him. He will not go to the grocery store. The crowds, the noise, the sudden movements—he says it makes him feel “electric.” He has not been to a restaurant in five years. He eats the same meal every day: a ham sandwich and a can of Coke, alone, in the break room at work. He has no friends. The men he worked with on that building are ghosts to him. He never called them. He never went to the memorial service.

When I ask him about the day, he does not speak of fear. He speaks of anger. A cold, fixed anger at the men who did it, at the city, at the company that made him go back to work. But mostly, he is angry at himself. “I should have seen it coming,” he says. “I was the foreman. I should have known.” He cannot separate the randomness of the event from his own perceived failure. He believes, with a quiet certainty, that he is responsible.

He is not a man who cries. He is a man who sits, still and watchful, in a hard-backed chair, his eyes scanning the room even as he talks. He is waiting for something. He doesn’t know what. He only knows that the quiet of his life is not peace. It is a held breath.
